Case Name: In re the Klein Living Trust Dated 6/5/1980
Case No.: 24PR196490
INTRODUCTION
According to the operative first amended petition (“FAP”) filed on January 14, 2025,
petitioner Matthew L. Klein (“Petitioner”), is a beneficiary of the Klein Living Trust dated
June 5, 1980, as amended and restated (the “Trust”) and an heir and successor-in-interest to
Paula P. Klein (“Settlor”), the settlor and sole beneficiary of the Trust until her passing in
September 2022. Respondent Cara Vainish (“Respondent”) is the current trustee of the Trust
and became the sole trustee in 2018 after the alleged incapacity of the Settlor.
The Trust holds three parcels of real property: (1) 10164 Vista Drive, Cupertino, CA
95014 bearing Santa Clara County Assessor’s Parcel Number 316-24-037-01 (the “Vista
Property”); (2) 11625 Oak Spring Court, Cupertino, CA 95014, bearing Santa Clara County
Assessor’s Parcel Number 366-52-073 (the “Oak Spring Property”); and (3) 22272 Cupertino
Road, Cupertino, CA 95014, bearing Santa Clara County Assessor’s Parcel Number 326-50-
030 (the “Cupertino Road Property”).
In 2019, Respondent retitled all three properties of the Trust in her name in accordance
with its terms. In 2020, Proposition 19 passed, ending the substantial property tax
reassessment exclusions available for parent-to-child transfers on or about February 15, 2021.
Respondent sought to distribute the Trust’s real properties to avoid the effect of the impending
changes to the property tax assessment rules. From December 2020 to early February 2021,
Petitioner and Respondent corresponded regarding the transfer of the Trust properties and how
the income derived from the properties would need to be maintained for the Settlor’s sole
benefit until her passing through life estate agreements. Respondent e-mailed Petitioner with a
fully executed and notarized deed for the Cupertino Road Property dated January 22, 2021 and
stated that she would provide him with the original on the condition that Petitioner would agree
that the rental income of the property would be paid to Settlor (i.e. the life estate agreement).
Petitioner did not agree to execute the life estate agreement.
When the Settlor died in September 2022, the Trust became irrevocable and ready for
final administration and distribution. In an email to Respondent’s counsel, Petitioner’s counsel
informally requested the original January 22, 2021 deed to Petitioner’s property and an
accounting of Respondent’s administration of the Trust. Respondent provided a deed dated
September 19, 2023 instead.
On January 18, 2024, Petitioner received a “Notice of Proposed Escape Assessment”
from the Office of the Assessor for Santa Clara County (the “Assessor”) and discovered that
Respondent had recorded the September 19, 2023 deed over his protest.
The FAP seeks instruction compelling Respondent to provide (1) formal accounting;
and (2) the January 22, 2021 trust transfer deed to Petitioner. In the alternative, the FAP
alleges Respondent breached her fiduciary obligations to Settlor and/or committed financial
elder abuse when Respondent transferred the real properties, eliminating Settlor’s rights to
receive all principal under the Trust and to modify the distribution of properties through the
Trust. The FAP specifically alleges that Respondent distributed the Trust properties to herself
and Petitioner despite knowing the terms of the Trust, consequently depriving Settlor of her
property rights in the Vista Property and Oak Spring Property. Notwithstanding the life estate
agreements, Settlor was deprived of a fee simple interest in the Vista Property and Oak Spring
Property. Furthermore, Respondent failed to record the life estate agreements with the
Assessor to retain the benefits of protection from property tax reassessment.
On November 7, 2025, Petitioner issued a Deposition Subpoena for Personal
Appearance and Production of Documents and Things to the Assessor relating to Respondent’s
transfer of Settlor’s rights in the Trust’s real properties prior to Proposition 19 coming into
effect (the “Subpoena”).
Currently before the court is Respondent’s motion to quash Petitioner’s subpoena.
Petitioned filed a timely opposition, and Respondent filed a timely reply.
DISCUSSION
I. Preliminary Matters
A. Request for Judicial Notice
Respondent requests judicial notice of the following documents in support of her
motion to quash:
• Exhibit A: Matthew Klein’s Petition for Instruction Compelling Trustee to
Account, and to Provide Original Trust Transfer Deed to Beneficiary, filed
January 23, 2024
• Exhibit B: Trustee Cara Vainish’s Response and Objection to Matthew Klein’s
Petition for Instruction Compelling Trustee to Account, and to Provide Original
Trust Transfer Deed to Beneficiary, filed March 6, 2024
• Exhibit C: Matthew Kelin’s First Amended Petition for Petition for Instruction
Compelling Trustee to Account, and to Provide Original Trust Transfer Deed to
Beneficiary, or, in the Alternative, Against Trustee for (1) Financial Elder
Abuse; and (2) Breaches of Fiduciary Duty Damages, and Attorneys’ Fees, filed
January 14, 2025.
As these documents are part of the record in this action, the Court GRANTS
Respondent’s request for judicial notice. (Evid. Code, § 452, subd. (d).)
B. Timeliness of the Motion
Petitioner argues within his separate statement that the motion is untimely as it was
filed on the eve of when the deposition should have taken place. There is, however, no
proscribed time requirement for filing a motion to quash under Code of Civil Procedure section
1987.1, the motion need only be “reasonably made”. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1987.1, subd. (a).)
Petitioner cites Lee v. Swansboro Country Property Owners Assn. (2007) 151 Cal.App.4th 575
(Lee) for the proposition that the statute contemplates proactive action, and thus, there was no
reason for Respondent’s withholding of the motion other than to delay. In Lee, the appellate
court reversed a trial court’s denial of a motion to quash a subpoena duces tecum on the ground
of untimeliness because the motion was filed a week before the judgment debtor’s
examination. (Id. at p. 583.) In opposition, Respondent cites Unzipped Apparel, LLC v.
Bader (2007) 156 Cal.App.4th 123, 135 (Unzipped), wherein the appellate court declined to
construe the “reasonably made” to mean a motion is timely when it is brought within
reasonable time. In so doing, the appellate court noted, “the Legislature knows how to use
‘reasonable time’ when it wants to refer to a temporal limit.” (Id. at p. 135, italics in original.)
The Court will follow the guidance of Unzipped and reach the merits of this motion.
II. Legal Standard
California Code of Civil Procedure Section 1987.1 provides that the Court “may make
an order quashing the subpoena entirely, modifying it, or directing compliance with it upon
those terms or conditions as the court shall declare, including protective orders.” (Code. Civ.
Proc., § 1987, subd. (a).)
“[A] civil litigant’s right to discovery is broad. (Williams v. Superior Court (2017) 3
Cal.5th 531, 541.) “[A]ny party may obtain discovery regarding any matter, not privileged, that
is relevant to the subject matter involved in the pending action or to the determination of any
motion made in that action, if the matter either is itself admissible in evidence or appears
reasonably calculated to lead to the discovery of admissible evidence.” (Code Civ. Proc., §
2017.010.) “In the context of discovery, evidence is ‘relevant’ if it might reasonably assist a
party in evaluating its case, preparing for trial, or facilitating a settlement. Admissibility
is not the test, and it is sufficient if the information sought might reasonably lead to other,
admissible evidence.” (Glenfed Development Corp. v. Super. Ct. (1997) 53 Cal.App.4th 1113,
1117.) “Any doubts regarding relevance are generally resolved in favor of allowing the
discovery.” (Mercury Interactive Corp. v. Klein (2007) 158 Cal.App.4th 60, 98.)
As the objecting party, Respondent generally bears the burden of justifying her
objections to the subpoenas.1 (See Kirkland v. Superior Court (2002) 95 Cal.App.4th 92,
98; Coy v. Superior Court of Contra Costa County (1962) 58 Cal.2d 210, 220 (Coy); Fairmont
Ins. Co. v. Super. Ct. (2000) 22 Cal. 4th 245, 255.)
III. Analysis
Respondent clarifies that the present motion to quash concerns Attachment 4 of the
Subpoena, which seeks the personal appearance and testimony of the Assessor’s person most
qualified (“PMQ”) on eleven topics. Respondent contends that the Subpoena seeks
information that is irrelevant to the dispute and not reasonably calculated to lead to the
discovery of admissible evidence. Respondent further asserts that the Subpoena was issued to
punish, burden, harass, and annoy.
Petitioner’s subpoena generally seeks the testimony of the Assessor’s PMQ on the
following topics:
1 The parties disagree on whether Respondent or Petitioner has the burden of demonstrating relevancy for
purposes of a motion to quash. The Court concludes that Respondent, as the objecting party, has the burden of
establishing the irrelevancy of the topics. (See Coy, supra, 58 Cal.2d at p. 220.)
• Transactions and internal reviews or investigations of the Trust’s three
properties. (Topic Nos. 1, 5)
• Communications by Respondent on behalf of Settlor concerning the Trust’s
three properties. (Topic No. 2.)
• The process, policies, and procedures of the Assessor for recording, processing,
and maintaining records related to property transactions, assessments, and
ownership changes for parent-to-child reassessment exclusion claims and any
continued real property interest a transferor may have in a transferred property.
(Topic Nos. 3-4.)
• The process, policies, and procedures of the Assessor for investigating and
resolving circumstances concerning the failure to report a transferor’s continued
income interest in real property. (Topic No. 6.)
• The impact of a contract providing a life estate to a transferor on any potential
change of ownership of a subject property to the transferee. (Topic No. 7.)
• Whether a life estate agreement for Settlor’s benefit invalidated any
reassessment exclusion for the Trust’s three properties. (Topic No. 8.)
• The penalties or interests a party may incur for omitting or misrepresenting the
life estate agreements when filing for a reassessment exclusion. (Topic Nos. 9-
10.)
• Where a party has intentionally omitted the life estate agreement on a property
or purposefully misled the Assessor, the parameters, metrics, and protocols the
Assessor uses to determine if the action should be reported to the Santa Clara
County District Attorney’s Office. (Topic No. 11.)
(Declaration of Leila Sockolov, Ex. A [“Subpoena”], Attachment 4.)
Respondent’s relevancy and harassment objections appear to arise from the Subpoena’s
characterization of this action:
This action under which this deposition subpoena is issued includes material
questions as to whether Petitioner [sic] CARA VAINISH either omitted
information, misrepresented information, or either negligently or purposefully
provided false information to the OFFICE OF THE ASSESSOR, COUNTY OF
SANTA CLARA, with respect to certain rights held by, or on behalf of, her
mother PAULA KLEIN, in order to manufacture a change in ownership with
respect to the VISTA PROPERTY and the OAK SPRINGS PROPERTY prior
to the termination of the parent-to-child reassessment exclusion that arose due to
Prop 19.
(Subpoena, p. 6.)
Respondent asserts that the representation is false and the “fabricated question” of
whether Respondent made misrepresentations to the Assessor is unrelated to the claims and
allegations in the FAP. The FAP alleges however,
Cara assured Matthew that these transfers [of the properties to Petitioner and
Respondent] were allowed for under the terms of the Trust (which was false),
that the structure of the proposed life estate agreements would successfully
allow the transfer of the property tax basis (which was also false), and that Paula
would retain the exact same rights and benefits as before (which was false yet a
third time).
As the existence of the life estate eliminates any change of ownership, Matthew
is informed, believes and thereon alleges that the actual execution of the life
estate agreements that Cara drafted specifically removed the very benefit she
sought to provide for herself. Furthermore, the existence of such agreements
could only have been withheld from the County Assessor through purposeful
omissions, so Matthew believes and alleges that even further liabilities to the
Trust may exist from Cara’s actions.
(FAP, ¶¶ 10, 29, fn. 5.)
Respondent also maintains that the information sought is irrelevant because it does not
concern whether Respondent deeded the Cupertino Road Property via the January 22, 2021
grant deed or whether Respondent breached her fiduciary duties by distributing properties to
herself before her mother passed—i.e., the issues raised by the FAP. Moreover, the FAP does
not allege (1) whether the Trust properties should have been assessed; (2) whether the Trust
properties should have received the reassessment exclusion; or (3) whether Petitioner incurred
penalties or interest for using the life estate agreement. In fact, Respondent contends,
Petitioner did not utilize a life estate agreement or file for the reassessment exclusion, and
Respondent’s proposed life estate agreement is not the basis of the breach of fiduciary duty
claim.
In opposition, Petitioner asserts that the information sought is relevant to the First
Amended Petition because the validity of the life estate agreements is central in establishing
that Respondent breached her fiduciary duties as Trustee. Specifically, Respondent’s creation,
promotion, and execution of the life estate agreements—in addition to refusal to record the life
estate agreements—were breaches of fiduciary duty and ineffective in generating the benefits
that Respondent had claimed. Indeed, the FAP alleges that Respondent engaged in self-dealing
by distributing Vista Property and Oak Spring Property to avail herself of the property tax
basis, while depriving Settlor of the various property rights. (FAP, ¶¶ 29, 33.) Furthermore,
Petitioner argues, the FAP seeks damages related to the breaches of fiduciary duty, breaches of
trust, financial elder abuse, in addition to attorneys’ fees and double damages. If the life estate
agreements were ineffective or invalid, Petitioner claims that Respondent should be liable for
the resulting damages and for depriving Settlor of an identifiable real property right (i.e. fee
simple interest to a life estate interest).
On reply, Respondent argues that the Settlor, Trust, and Petitioner would not be
damaged if the Assessor determines Respondent’s two properties are not entitled to the
reassessment exclusion. With respect to Settlor and Trust, Respondent asserts that she alone
would be liable for the property taxes because Respondent’s executed life estate agreements
protected Settlor’s interest in the income generated by the properties while distributing the
properties to Respondent. With respect to Petitioner, Respondent argues that Petitioner could
not be harmed because he never executed the life estate agreement. The court agrees.
Accordingly, the court finds that Respondent, as the objecting party, has met the burden
of establishing the irrelevancy of the majority of the topics The Court, however, does find
Topics 1 and 2, regarding transactions and communications about the specific properties to be
appropriate and relevant.
The Court therefore GRANTS in part Respondent’s motion to quash Topic Nos. 3-11.
The Court DENIES the motion to quash with respect to topics 1 and 2. The subpoena is
modified to remove the latter 9 topics.
